newsitem.title: UK: Russia jumbo mark Eurobond well-received.
newsitem.headline: Russia jumbo mark Eurobond well-received.

text.p: Russia raised 2.0 billion marks ($1.2 billion) on Thursday in its second-ever international bond issue, which was well-received by investors.
"There has been a very good reception of the Russia Eurobond," an official at joint lead manager Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said.

The seven-year bond was priced to yield 3.70 percentage points over German government bonds and will pay an annual interest rate of nine percent. Credit Suisse First Boston and Deutsche Morgan Grenfell underwrote the bond.

Russia's bond comes against a background of soft market conditions, with demand for high-yielding bonds weaker due to sharp price falls triggered by worries of a U.S. interest rate rise, bankers said.
But bankers said the rarity value of Russian debt boosted demand for the issue.
"A lot of investors would not have bought a bond by a Latin American country because there have been so many deals from them in marks," a dealer at a U.S. bank in Frankfurt said.
"They bought Russia because it offered a rare chance to diversify into Eastern Europe," he said.
The nine percent coupon and high launch spread were also important factors, he said.
"The attractive terms made up for the slightly larger-than-expected size. The initial reception has been good, but we will only be able to tell in the next few days where the price goes," he said.
Russia has high speculative grade ratings, Ba2 from Moody's Investors Service and BB minus from Standard and Poor's.
The mark bond followed Russia's successful $1.0 billion five-year debut deal in November, its first foreign bond since the 1917 revolution.
The dollar bond, the largest debut bond ever issued, was heavily oversubscribed, and Russia was able to raise two to three times more than it had originally planned.
Similarly, demand for the mark paper proved robust, with Russia initially expected to raise only a billion marks.
The Deutsche official said around 75 percent of its 800 million mark allocation has been sold.
CSFB officials said a large percentage of their bonds had also been placed. "We had a fantastic start to the deal and have sold bonds to Asia and throughout Europe," a syndicate manager at CSFB said.
"We are delighted with the way it has gone. The deal is not fully placed yet, which is common in marks, but the follow-through demand has been very, very strong," he said.

Thursday's issue has opened up another source of funds for Russia, which plans to borrow another $2.0 billion this year, and will enable other Russian borrowers and countries in the region to also tap these investors.
"If this deal works and performs well, it will set the stage for other borrowers to follow," the CSFB official said.
Buyers of high-yielding mark Eurobonds tend to be smaller German and Benelux investors, in contrast to mainly institutional buyers of Eurobonds denominated in dollars. ($1=1.7153 Mark)
